analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments next in number 1800, United States against Sotelo. 72 days ago. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, this federal income tax and bankruptcy case comes here on a writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit. It presents the question whether the statutory liability equal to unpaid taxes withheld from employees' wages, which is imposed by Section 6672 of the Internal Revenue Code, upon persons who are required to collect and pay over such taxes but who willfully fail to do so, is dischargeable under Section 17 of the Bankruptcy Act. We submit that this liability is not dischargeable and that the Court of Appeals erred in so holding. The facts are relatively simple and undisputed. On June 26, 1973, Onufre J. Sotelo and Son Masonry Incorporated, a corporation, was adjudicated a bankrupt. The president of this corporation was respondent Onufre J. Sotelo, and the secretary of the corporation was his wife, Naomi. About ten days later, on July 5, Onufre J. Sotelo and Naomi Sotelo were adjudicated bankrupts themselves, and their cases were thereafter consolidated in the bankruptcy court. Later that year, in November, the government filed a claim in the individual bankruptcy cases for unpaid withholding taxes amounting to $40,000. This claim was later reduced to $32,000. The claim was based upon Section 6672 of the Internal Revenue Code, which I have referred to as imposing a statutory liability on so-called responsible officers of a corporation who are required to collect withholding taxes and pay them over but who willfully fail to do so. Mr. Smith, what section is it that requires the responsible officers to collect? I agree that 6672 imposes a penalty upon those who are required to collect, but I'm curious to know what section it is that requires them to collect. Well, Mr. Justice Rehnquist, Section 6671B defines a person as used in this subchapter, which includes an officer or employee of a corporation. And Section 3402 of the Code, which we set forth at page 3A of the appendix to our brief, says, except as otherwise provided in this section, every employer making payment of wages shall deduct and withhold upon such wages, a tax determined in accordance with tables prescribed by the secretary. So the requirement is that these were statutory. Arnifred J. Sotelo was a statutory person under the code, and he was, the employer was the corporation, and he acted on behalf of the corporation. He was required to collect and pay over these taxes. You say those two sections together not only require the employer to pay, but make one in Sotelo's position responsible for paying over. Yes, and then if he fails to pay, Section 6672. I agree with that. Right. You think your first proposition is crystal clear? I think so, because he's acting on behalf of the employer. It says every employer making payment of wages, the corporation, corporations act through their offices, and under Section 6671B, the term person includes an officer of a, or employee of a corporation, or a member of employee of a partnership, et cetera, et cetera. I think that's clear, Mr. Chester. Perhaps it's already been covered in this colloquy, but is it not clear that the statute requires the employer to withhold the employee's portion from payment, Social Security taxes, for example, or withholding, and that if he fails to do it, the employer is responsible? That's right. That's right. If he fails... He has made, Congress has made the employer the tax collector, has he not? Exactly. And if the employer, as in this case, the typical situation where the Section 6672 liability arises, is where the employer is a corporation which goes bankrupt and is no longer, has assets to pay, and then the Congress has determined that the collection agent, the responsible collection agent, who made the decision to willfully prefer other creditors over the United States, he becomes personally liable for these taxes. And, in fact, in the bankruptcy court in this case, there was a trial as to whether Onufre J. Sotelo and or Naomi Sotelo were responsible officers under Section 6672. And the trial judge found that Onufre was a responsible officer, but not Naomi Sotelo. And that's undisputed, that he is a responsible officer and that he has this liability. The assets of the bankruptcy estate were insufficient to satisfy the government's tax claim. The government thereupon levied on a $10,000 fund that had been set aside outside the bankruptcy estate as Onufre J. Sotelo's homestead exemption under Illinois law. And Onufre J. Sotelo objected to the levy on the grounds that the homestead exemption belonged to his wife, Naomi, and not himself. But he also argued, and that is the question before the court, that the Section 6672 liability for unpaid withholding taxes was a dischargeable compensatory penalty rather than a tax, and that his after-acquired property should be insulated from collection. Mr. Smith, strictly speaking, is the 6672 liability a tax liability or a liability for something equivalent to the amount of the tax? The reason I ask, following up on Justice Rehnquist's question, is that Section 3403 describes the person's liable for the tax, and it only identifies the employer. The employer shall be liable for the payment of the tax required to be withheld and so forth. I think what that is is that Section 3403 provides that the employer shall be liable for the payment of the tax in the first instance, but that Section 6672 provides for backup liability when the employer doesn't pay for the tax. We have argued at length in our brief, and I believe... Is it the question, I suppose, is whether the backup liability is, strictly speaking, a tax liability? I think it is a tax liability, although that is... Congress used the term penalty, but the authorities, apart from the decision below in this case, are unanimous, not only two circuits, but all the district courts, and the treatises are unanimous in describing this as a tax liability. Had this question arisen prior to 1966 when Section 17 was amended? This question had arisen prior to 1966 in cases like the Sherwood case, which we cite in our brief in the Eastern District of New York case, and the court had held that this was a tax liability and not a penalty. But that is an alternative... I want to emphasize that that is an alternative argument that we make. We think that our primary argument in this case is that this is... This liability is not dischargeable under Section 17A1E of the Bankruptcy Act, which was added to Section 17 in 1966. But before I mention that, I just want to briefly summarize what the courts below have... Just before you leave this, doesn't the code also say that penalties shall be levied and assessed and collected like taxes? Like taxes, yes. So they're to be treated as taxes? They're treated like taxes. That's 6671? 6671A. And, in fact, the Second Circuit in Bata v. Scanlon has held that they're subject to the Anti-Injunction Act, like taxes. Which defines taxes in a different way, does it not, than the code? The Anti-Injunction Act? I mean, you can't carry over the Second Circuit holding A.O. Ipse, so to speak, to this case, can you? Well, but I think it's persuasive. I mean, as Justice White has said, I mean, these things are always treated as taxes. The Internal Revenue Service endeavors to make sure that these things are only collected once when the corporation fails. They're only collected once from the officer. I don't think that there's any doubt that the way that they're treated administratively and the way the courts have regarded them, they're always treated as taxes, notwithstanding the penalty. The Section 671 says, any reference in this title to tax imposed by this title shall be deemed also to refer to the penalties and liability. Penalties and liability is imposed by the subject. That's right. That's right. But I would submit, and I don't want to belabor the point because I think it's covered in our brief, that despite the penalty denomination, these things are always treated as taxes, and the courts, apart from this court, has so helped. Mr. Smith, tell me the basis for your statement that the Internal Revenue Service collects only once as a matter of policy. Is there a... The basis of our statement for that is an opinion, a policy statement, which we cited page 30 at our brief, policy statement P-5-60. Subject to change tomorrow. What? Subject to change tomorrow. Well, quite frankly, I've been working in this area for quite a while, and I've never heard of any instance where the Internal Revenue Service has attempted to collect Section 6672 liability more than once. No, but you've heard of many instances where the Internal Revenue Service changes its mind. Oh, absolutely. But I cannot... It's hard for me to imagine changing its mind in this context when, given the authorities which have held its attacks, which are rendered at the urging of the government. In any event, the bankruptcy court held that the Section 672 liability was non-dischargeable under Section 17 of the Bankruptcy Act, and the district court affirmed. And the Court of Appeals reversed. It held that Section 17A1E, which is our primary argument before the court today, was not applicable, and it also held that the liability was a penalty and not a tax. I want to begin by referring the Court to Section 17A1E because I think that its terms are explicit and cover this case. The pertinent language is set forth at pages 5A and going over to 6A of the appendix to our brief. The beginning of Section 17, the basic discharge provision, says a discharge in bankruptcy shall release a bankrupt from all of his provable debts, whether allowable in full, in part, except as such. And then there's an exception for taxes. And then it goes on to say, provided, however, that a discharge in bankruptcy shall not release a bankrupt from any taxes. And then if the court will turn over to page 6A and pick up at subsection E, which the bankrupt has collected or withheld from others as required by the laws of the United States or any state or political subdivision thereof, but has not paid over. So... And you're... Tell me again, you're... Answer the question of where you find the source of the requirement that the bankrupt, who is an officer and not the taxpayer, pay over. Well, the bankrupt... In the first instance... He was not liable for the taxes in the first instance. In the first instance, of course he wasn't liable. The corporation was liable. But the corporation did not pay them. He paid net... As the responsible officer, Arnafrae J. Sotelo paid net wages to his employees and benefited... Well, to the corporation's employees. The employees... The corporation was the employer. Oh, absolutely. Yeah, right, right. They were not his employees. No, they were not. It was the corporation's employees. But acting on behalf of the corporation, Arnafrae J. Sotelo paid net wages to his employees and did not... They were not his employees. Right. And it, the corporation, okay, did not pay... Oh, I understand. It's the basis of the Seventh Circuit's opinion. I understand. It's nothing we can just forget about. No, I understand that. And I'm sorry if my nomenclature has been inaccurate. Well, it's the basis of the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals opinion. Yes, I know. The basis of the Seventh Circuit's Court of Appeals opinion is that it was the corporation's liability. That the corporation was the employer. And not, Arnafrae J. Sotelo's liability. But in our view, this ignores the very explicit legislative history extending over eight years in which the Treasury kept telling the Congress, and it set forth in our briefing in great detail, that it was, it resisted mightily the proposition that taxes and this Section 6672 liability would be made dischargeable in bankruptcy. And the Treasury's major submission to Congress, and it was made to the Judiciary Committees and to the Ways and Means and Finance Committees, was that there was an inequity in giving a responsible officer or a bankroll a discharge. Mr. Smith, before you tell us about the Treasury Department's objections to the 1966 legislation, why don't you tell us what the purpose of the 1966 amendment was? The purpose of the 1966 amendment was? The entire amendment, I mean. The entire amendment was as follows. It was to introduce a statute of limitations. Section 17A, before 1966. Wasn't it to ameliorate the harsh rule against the individual who had to pay and had a non-dischargeable tax obligation, regardless of how old it was? That was part of it. It was in order to protect the individual tax. That was part of it. Congress was interested in providing a statute of limitations for stale tax claims in bankruptcy, because before 1966, tax claims were not dischargeable, and they were forever subject to collectible out of it. And that was inequitable to individuals, but not to corporations, because corporations would just be dissolved. Corporations, right. And Congress. It was to provide protection to individuals, to bankrupt individuals. Exactly. And that's, Mr. Justice Stevens, that was introduced in Section 17A1, because it says, except as such as our taxes, which became legally due in owing by the bankrupt to the United States or to any state or subdivision thereof within three years preceding bankruptcy. But there was another purpose in adding Section 17A1E. The Treasury Department was terribly concerned about mounting delinquencies in trust fund taxes, because it properly pointed out to the pertinent committees that there was an inequity in giving a bankrupt to discharge for failure to pay, not to pay his own taxes, but for failure to keep intact money which he had obtained from others as a trustee for the government. But in 1958, Congress felt that a criminal penalty would suffice, and they enacted Section 7202 of the Code, which was provided for a criminal penalty for willfully failing to pay these things, pay these trust fund taxes over. But the point is... The Department letter expressly identified the problem as problems where they collected the money from third persons and converted such monies to their own use. Exactly. Well, now, that didn't happen here, did it? Well, of course it happened here, because what happened here was that the employees were paid net wages, and the corporation benefited from the fact that it did not pay the withholding taxes over. But it's not the corporation's liability that we're dealing with. Exactly. But then, by operation of the statutory provisions in the Code 6671-B and 6672, this liability becomes Onufre J. Sotelo's liability. And the point is... But did Onufre J. Sotelo convert these funds to his own personal use? In the sense that he contributed them, or, I mean, that the funds were contributed or remained in the corporation, which he ran... Is that the normal use? Is that the normal way you think of a corporate officer converting corporate assets to his own use? In the sense that he was... In the sense that his business was able to continue to use these funds would seem to me to be a use of... It's... Or if corporations are on you. Mr. Smith? You say that 6671-B on page 4A of your brief, it is the provision you rely on that imposes liability upon a corporate officer to pay taxes that are owed by the corporation. And yet, that, as I read it, simply says it includes an officer or employee of a corporation or a member of an employee of a partnership who is under a duty to perform the act. In other words, it speaks the same way 6672 does. Both of them speak of people who are already under a duty. I still want to know, where does Sotelo's original duty to pay taxes on behalf of the corporation arise from? His original duty to pay taxes on behalf of the corporation arises as the principal officer of the employer. Well, what provision of the statute tells us that? Well, the 3402, if you turn back a page, in 3403, say that every employer making payment of wages, and then it says the employer shall be liable. Now... Well, the employer here is a corporation. Exactly. And we're not Sotelo. Exactly. But corporations are legal entities. They have to operate through their principle... through people. Well, then you're not relying on any specific code language. No, I mean, I think that, you know, the case laws is clear that in fixing 6672 liability, they look to the person who was responsible... Who would be responsible in a common law... In a common law situation, you know, to make the decisions. And here that was on a free... The bankruptcy court found that that was on a free J. Sotelo. And there's no dispute about that. We submit that there was no dispute that he was a person required to collect, truthfully account for, and pay over the withholding taxes. And he collected those taxes by paying net wages to his corporation's employees. And in our view, he is a bankrupt who has collected or withheld taxes from others as required by the laws of the United States, but who has not paid them over within Section 17A1E. Now, I think that it is not without significance that the House report... I don't suppose the government could just pick anybody at random in the corporation and put him in... and impose this kind of liability on him. Say that... I'm sorry, I didn't... The government just can't pick anybody in the corporation at random. Oh, no. They should identify and must identify the people who, as the corporation is organized, has the duty of paying taxes. Exactly. Exactly. That has to be the person who makes the final decision, who says, well, we have a tax liability here, and then we have... Why doesn't it be the person who makes the final decision? Why can't it be the bookkeeper who's charged with the duty to make the deductions and write out the checks? Well, if the bookkeeper exercises untrammeled authority... What in this statute says it's got to be untrammeled authority? Well, I mean, I would suggest, Mr. Justice Stevens, that if the president of a corporation said to the bookkeeper, don't pay the taxes this month, pay the ex-corporation... The bookkeeper's duty is to withhold and collect and pay over, under your view. That's what she does, eight hours a day, seven days a week. I suppose as a technical matter she could be liable, but it would seem to me that she's being... her authority is being circumscribed and being taken away from her. What in the statute tells us who has to have what authority? I still don't think you've quite answered, Mr. Justice Reinhard. Well, I think that the case law indicates that it's the person... The case law on this court? Well, there's no case law on this court, but, I mean, the Uniform Court of Appeals case law indicates that it's the person in the corporation, and, indeed, there could be more than one, who makes the decision that the taxes are not going to be paid at this time because the corporation doesn't have enough money, or they don't have enough money at this time, so we're going to postpone payment of the taxes, and it's going to be... We're going to willfully prefer other creditors. And that decision under Section 66... What has willfully preferring other creditors got to do with it? Nothing in the statute says you're only liable if you willfully prefer other creditors. You're liable if you don't pay. That's right. That's right. And why do we talk about willfully preferring other creditors? Well, because normally that's the way... Is this the department policy, is it, or is it statutory command? Oh, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, because in the normal situation, if you've got the money, you pay your taxes. I use that term because the case law uses that term. You're right. If you have all the money in the world and you just decide you're not going to pay withholding taxes, of course you're going to be personally liable, assuming that the corporation then goes bankrupt. I do want to point out to the court that it is not without significance that the current Congress... I understand that the views of one Congress can't be attributed to another strictly, but that the current Congress regards it to settle, that Section 17A1E renders the Section 6672 liability non-dischargeable. There's a massive codification of the bankruptcy bill, which has just passed the House and which is being considered by the Senate, and at page 22, we refer to a 1977 committee report, which I would like to quote. It's very short. It says, The current Bankruptcy Act renders non-dischargeable all taxes which the bankrupt is collected or withheld from others, but is not paid over. Thus, withholding taxes are accorded an unlimited priority under present law. The priority even includes the 100 percent, and they use the word penalty in quotes, imposed under the Internal Revenue Code. The present unlimited priority is justified by the notion that withholding taxes are held in trust. In other words, the same rationale that the Treasury pressed Congress in the mid-1960s, that a bankrupt should not benefit from his failure to honor the statutory trust of these trust fund taxes. But that wouldn't answer the question of whether Sotelo himself is subject to 6672 liability, would it? I wouldn't answer the question, but that question is not in this case, because the bankruptcy, it's absolutely assumed that, I mean, it's... Assumed is a good word for it. No, it's given. I mean, it's... The lower courts have held, and the Sotelo does not contend to the contrary, that he's subject to Section 6672 liability. The question is whether it's dischargeable. I think the current Congress regards... It is settled that Section 17A1E was designed to not only reach as the corporate bankrupt, because, as we point out, Congress recognized that in a liquidating bankruptcy, the corporation disappears. So it would have been rather futile to enact Section 17A1E in order to preserve trust fund tax liabilities post-bankruptcy. Why do you say a corporation, quote, disappears, close quote, in a liquidating bankruptcy? Well, in a liquidate... As my understanding is that a corporation that liquidates and goes out of existence in a liquidating bankruptcy and distributes all of its assets, even if it reconstitutes itself under different ownership, is a different entity. Well, if it goes out of existence, it goes out of existence. But what if it doesn't? Well, if it doesn't go out of existence... I mean, why does it do so inevitably? It doesn't do so inevitably, but it does so in many instances. And Congress recognized that... In many instances, bankrupts die, too. Oh, absolutely. But what Congress was interested in was making sure of enhancing the Treasury's opportunity to collect these trust fund taxes from either the corporation, if it didn't disappear, or from the responsible officer because of his statutory liability, which we submit does not disappear upon bankruptcy and is non-dischargeable. There's nothing in the bankruptcy law that prevents the El Fideldo Realty Company, a bankrupt, after it has turned over all its assets from getting a new board of directors and keeping right on as the El Fideldo Realty Company is. Oh, no. I don't mean to suggest that every corporation that undergoes bankruptcy disappears. But as we point out in our brief, Congress observed that although a corporate bankrupt is theoretically not discharged, the corporation normally ceases to exist upon bankruptcy and unsatisfied tax claims, as well as all other unsatisfied claims, are without further recourse, even though the enterprise may continue... Mr. Chris, didn't the United States file a claim in Sotelo's bankruptcy? In the individual's bankruptcy? Yes. And it was approved? It was approved. It was allowed and approved. It was allowed by the judge, not objected to. And the only question is dischargeability. Exactly. Exactly. That's the only question before the court. Mr. Smith, am I not... Maybe it's in misapprehension, but wasn't $7,900 of that claim not allowed by the bankruptcy judge? That's right. That's right. And what is the reason for that? I'm not sure the record doesn't disclose it, but I assume that... But the amount that's at issue here, Sotelo's liability for whatever his conduct was is not disputed? Not disputed. I would like to save the remaining time, if I may. Very well, Mr. Smith. Mr. Balsh. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court. On behalf of the respondents, Onafrae J. Sotelo and Naomi Sotelo, we submit that the Section 6672 penalty is an obligation that is dischargeable in the personal bankruptcy of the individual against whom it is assessed. And reaching a conclusion on this issue, we... Could I just ask you, is there any question about the validity of the claim and the bankruptcy? There is no question, Your Honor. That was determined at the bankruptcy judge level, and neither side appealed from it. Neither side was happy with it because the government wanted more and Sotelo wanted less, but I believe we have to take it as a fact at this point. But you don't now contest that Sotelo owed the money to the United States? I don't contest that, Your Honor. That was the very next thing I was going to say, that in reaching a decision on this case, it is important to distinguish between the concept of liability and the concept of dischargeability. Yes. In any event, he owed the money. And if there had been money to distribute in the estate at 50 cents on the dollar, 50 cents on the dollar at least would have gone to the United States. Your Honor, I wish to make the point that this was an asset case. The government filed and proved a claim in the personal bankruptcy. That claim was allowed for a substantial sum. The government obtained a dividend from the personal assets. Right. Thanks. However, those assets were not sufficient to pay the claim in full, and that's what brings us here. Right. Now, you began by some discussion about Section 6672 liability, but I'm not sure you finished your sentence. Would you give me that again? I wanted to make the distinction between the liability under Section 6672 and its dischargeability. And I'm careful, and I hope I don't have a slip of the tongue somewhere in this discussion that I, heaven forbid, call that a tax. I call it an obligation. It is an obligation for a penalty, and we say that it is considerably different than the obligation for a tax. And the importance of that distinction becomes apparent when we go on to look at Section 17A1 of the Bankruptcy Act. Now, a right to a discharge in bankruptcy is a rather sweeping privilege that Congress has extended to all bankrupts. And you start out with a general rule that a discharge in bankruptcy shall release a bankrupt from all of his provable debts, whether allowable in full or in part, except such as are. And then there are some exceptions. Now, we point out that the facts relate in this case that at the government's instance a claim was proved in the personal bankruptcy. It was allowed in part, and therefore we squarely come within the general rule that this claim is a dischargeable claim, and therefore releases the bankrupt from all of his provable debts and so forth. Now, if we are to say that one of the exceptions applies here, we say that the general rule of statutory construction is that one who asserts an exception to a recognized general rule has the burden of showing that you come within the exception. And we feel we've clearly shown we come within the general rule. So let's examine the exceptions and see if the government has met this burden of coming within one of them. Now, the primary exception that the government relies upon in this case is the exception in 17A1, which accepts taxes. So we're then met with the question, what is the nature of the obligation under Section 6672? Well, the first place to look, I would suggest, is Section 6672. What characterization did Congress itself put upon this obligation when they wrote Section 6672? They say that certain people who are defined in that section, and we concede that Sotelo is one of them, shall, in addition to other penalties provided by law, be liable to a penalty. Now, clearly, they're talking penalty. They do not say that the individual is liable for the tax. This is not a tax on Mr. Sotelo. He did not file any returns. He didn't have a tax identification number in this capacity. The corporation was liable for the tax. And if the corporation... There are provisions in the federal tax laws making certain parties secondarily liable for a tax, are there not? That is correct, Your Honor, and I would say this is one of them. Like the donee for a... You'd say this is not one of them. Like the donee for a gift tax is secondarily liable for the gift tax. At least that used to be the law. Oh, a transferee liability type of thing? Transferee liability. Yes, Your Honor. And that's secondary liability for the tax. But here your point is this is not secondary liability for a tax, but rather a penalty. Thank you for correcting my slip of the tongue there, Your Honor. Well, isn't that a... In other words, if Congress knows how to say a secondary liability for a tax, it does know how to say so because it has said so in certain... That is correct. They've made it very clear in other contexts that if they want the individual to be directly liable as a taxpayer... Or secondarily liable for a tax. They can say that. I don't think they said it in Section 6672. What do you think is the significance in the very context that you're just discussing of the language... Shall, in addition to other penalties provided by law, be liable to a penalty equal to the total amount of the tax evaded? Haven't they... Doesn't this language equate the tax and the penalty? That language, Your Honor, shows to the person enforcing this section how the amount of the penalty is calculated. Doesn't it make them all one? What? Doesn't it make them one on the same thing? No, Your Honor. They could have just as well left out the words, a penalty equal to the... And that is one of the points we wish to make. That in construing a statute, if there are two possible ways to look at it, the preferred way is the way that gives meaning to each of the words that are in there. And if you construe it as simply saying a direct liability for the tax, you're rendering meaningless the words, a penalty equal to the. Can it not be read as saying that Congress intended that one way or another we're going to get this tax? We're going to get this tax which was in trust and held in trust, and for these purposes we may call it a penalty. Your Honor, that brings me back to my primary point at the very outset, and that was we must be careful to distinguish between liability and dischargeability. The point that Your Honor's question makes is that Congress wanted this person liable for this amount of money. And non-dischargeable? No, dischargeability is the issue to be decided today. We have passed the point of liability. Yes. And doesn't this language, isn't this language directed at dischargeability? I would say, Your Honor, that if we can ascribe any motive at all to why they worded it in this rather peculiar fashion, I would say that it was put in there to show that there was some difference between the nature of this liability and the nature of a direct liability for the tax. What about the provision of 6671A that says that except as otherwise provided, any reference in this title to a tax shall be deemed to include the penalties? Now, if you can see that you've got a liability for a penalty, you look at the code, it says you should treat penalties like taxes. Now, you say that may be so for purposes of the code but not for purposes of bankruptcy? Your Honor has asked the question and has answered it because the section just cited refers in its operation to a particular title. And that's the whole problem with the approach of the government to this case and our approach. They're looking at this as a tax case. We think it's a bankruptcy case.
